reason: The sources provide multi-site verified facts detailing Galileo's 1610 telescopic discovery of Milky Way stars alongside ancient myths, etymology, and modern galactic structure.
story: For thousands of years, humans gazed at the glowing river arching across the night sky and wondered what it was. Greek mythology claimed it was milk spilled from the goddess Hera's breast, while scholars like Aristotle thought it was burning vapors in Earth's atmosphere. To the unaided human eye, it appeared as nothing more than a seamless, wispy cloud. Everything changed in 1610 when Galileo Galilei aimed his primitive spyglass at the celestial band. To his astonishment, the milky fog vanished, resolving into an overwhelming swarm of countless individual stars packed too tightly and faintly for the naked eye to separate. Today we know our solar system sits inside a massive barred spiral disk containing hundreds of billions of stars and planets, all orbiting a central supermassive black hole with a mass of about 4 million suns. That ghostly splash of milk wasn't a cloud—it was home.
angle: The faint white 'cloud' in our night sky is not vapor at all, but the blended glow of hundreds of billions of distant stars.

claims.claim: In 1610, Galileo Galilei used an optical telescope to observe the Milky Way.
Galileo discovered that the Milky Way's band is composed of countless individual faint stars rather than a continuous cloud.
Before Galileo's telescopic resolution, the Milky Way appeared to the unaided eye as a hazy, cloudy band of light.
The stars forming the Milky Way glow are so distant and close together in the sky that naked human eyes cannot resolve them individually.
Galileo published his revolutionary 1610 astronomical observations in the treatise Sidereus Nuncius (Starry Messenger).
In Greek myth, the Milky Way was said to have formed when Hera pushed baby Heracles away and her breast milk spilled across the sky.
The Classical Latin term 'via lactea' translates to milky road or milky way.
The word 'galaxy' is derived from the ancient Greek word for milk.
The Milky Way galaxy contains an estimated 100 billion to 400 billion stars.
The Milky Way is structured as a vast flattened disk of stars rather than a sphere.
Our Sun is located roughly halfway out toward the edge of the galaxy's disk, about 25,000 to 28,000 light-years from the center.
The Milky Way features a central bulge and spiral arms.
The center of the galaxy is marked by a supermassive black hole weighing approximately 4 million solar masses.
Interstellar cosmic dust clouds, such as the Great Rift, block background visible starlight across the galactic plane.
In 1785, William Herschel attempted to map the shape of the Milky Way by counting stars across different sky regions.
Herschel's map erroneously placed the Sun near the center of the galaxy due to dust obscuration.
Philosopher Immanuel Kant speculated that certain nebulae might be separate 'island universes' comparable to our own Milky Way.
Observations by Edwin Hubble in the 1920s proved that the Milky Way was just one of many distinct galaxies in the universe.

disputed: Herschel's star-counting partner: S2 explicitly attributes the 1785 star counts to sibling astronomers William and Caroline Herschel, while S1 mentions only William Herschel. A script should attribute William or say 'William and Caroline Herschel'.

Diameter of the Milky Way stellar disk: S1 cites an isophotal diameter of roughly 87,400 light-years, while S2 references modern measurements placing the disk at 120,000 light-years across. A script should state disk estimates vary between roughly 87,000 and 120,000 light-years.

The Heracles breastfeeding story: S1 notes two variants—one where Zeus secretly places the sleeping infant on Hera's breast, and another where Athena gives him to Hera. A script should simply state: 'According to Greek myth, Hera spilled milk while pushing away baby Heracles.'
